problem.text: Given $k \geq 1$, let $p_k$ denote the $k$-th smallest prime number. If $N$ is the number of ordered $4$-tuples $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive integers satisfying $abcd = \prod_{k=1}^{2023} p_k$ with $a < b$ and $c < d$, find $N \bmod 1000$.

steps.title: Where to start: every prime goes to exactly one of $a, b, c, d$
steps.body: Let $P = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_{2023}$. It is a product of $2023$ different primes, each appearing once. So a solution of $abcd = P$ is just a way of sending each prime to one of $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$. The conditions $a < b$ and $c < d$ concern the pairs $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ separately, so first decide which primes go to the pair $(a, b)$, that is, which primes divide $ab$.

your_turn.prompt: Ignoring the conditions $a < b$ and $c < d$, how many ordered $4$-tuples $(a, b, c, d)$ have $abcd = P$?
your_turn.answer: $4^{2023}$, since each of the $2023$ primes independently picks one of the four numbers.

steps.title: Count one pair with $a < b$
steps.body: Suppose exactly $i$ of the primes divide $ab$; there are $\binom{2023}{i}$ ways to pick them. Those $i$ primes can be split between $a$ and $b$ in $2^i$ ordered ways. When $i \ge 1$, $ab$ is a product of distinct primes, so it is not a perfect square and $a \ne b$; swapping $a$ and $b$ pairs the splits up, so exactly half, $2^{i-1}$, have $a < b$. The same reasoning gives $2^{2023 - i - 1} = 2^{2022 - i}$ choices for $(c, d)$ when $2023 - i \ge 1$.

your_turn.answer: If $i = 0$, then $ab = 1$, forcing $a = b = 1$, which breaks $a < b$. If $i = 2023$, then $cd = 1$ and $c = d = 1$, which breaks $c < d$.

steps.title: Add up over $i$
steps.body:
Each term has $2^{i-1} \cdot 2^{2022 - i} = 2^{2021}$, so
$$N = \sum_{i=1}^{2022} \binom{2023}{i} 2^{2021} = 2^{2021}\left(2^{2023} - 2\right).$$
Here we used $\sum_{i=0}^{2023} \binom{2023}{i} = 2^{2023}$ (count all subsets of the primes) and removed the $i = 0$ and $i = 2023$ terms, which are $1$ each.

your_turn.prompt: Rewrite $2^{2021}(2^{2023} - 2)$ by pulling a $2$ out of the parentheses.

steps.title: Mod $1000$: split into mod $8$ and mod $125$
steps.body: Since $1000 = 8 \cdot 125$ with no common factor, find $N$ mod $8$ and mod $125$. Mod $8$ it is $0$, because $2^{2022}$ is a multiple of $2^3$. Mod $125$, Euler's theorem gives $2^{100} \equiv 1$ (as $\varphi(125) = 100$), so $2^{2022} = (2^{100})^{20} \cdot 2^{22} \equiv 2^{22} \pmod{125}$.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Mod $125$, $N \equiv 54 \cdot (54 - 1) = 54 \cdot 53 = 2862 \equiv 2862 - 2750 = 112$. The number $112 = 8 \cdot 14$ is also $\equiv 0 \pmod 8$, so it satisfies both conditions and is the one remainder mod $1000$ that does. So $N \equiv 112 \pmod{1000}$. The answer is **$112$**.
